Asked Monday, May 8, 2023, during Teacher Appreciation Week at Beach School. Previously printed in the Piedmont Post on May 10, 2023. CATHERINE TRESCH-GOMEZ, 2nd grade I appreciate Ms. Ford because she comes up with a lot of fun techniques for math and writing. IZZY JAESCHKE, 2nd grade I appreciate Ms. Wighton for teaching me. The science project she just had us do was really fun. We made models of bees. RELIGION CORNER Advent Devotional By Rev. Jim Hopkins “Because of the tender mercy of our God, the dawn from on high will break upon us.” Luke 1:68-79 Once, when the priest Zechariah was attending to his duties at the temple in Jerusalem, the angel Gabriel appeared to him and announced that Zechariah and his wife Elizabeth, previously unable to bear a child, would soon be welcoming a son into their lives. Zechariah, whose name means “God remembers,” was naturally shocked and asked the angel if he knew what he was talking about. This challenge did not sit well with Gabriel and he rendered Zechariah unable to speak until the son promised to Elizabeth and he was born. Even when his son was born Zechariah couldn’t say a word until he wrote “His name is John.” Once he had regained his voice Zechariah began to praise God. His words are known as the “Benedictus,” Latin for the first words of his prayer, “Blessed be the Lord God of Israel.” Of the prayer, Amy-Jill Levine writes, “Zechariah’s prayer, like Mary’s Magnificat, is less a prediction than an assurance: God has acted in the past, and those actions have repercussions for the present and the future.” Towards the end of his prayer Zechariah speaks what, to me, are some of the most beautiful words in the entire Bible. “Because of the tender mercy of our God, the dawn from on high will break upon us.” What wonderful imagery. What an encouraging promise. What soaring hope. The tender mercy of God blesses us now and will bless us always. Words of comfort and joy. I am left to wonder what, after having been unable to speak for nine months, I would say upon regaining the ability to speak. Would I praise God like Zechariah did? Would I be able to lift a song of God’s tender mercy? articles.text: If you own real property in California, you must pay property taxes twice a year. The first installment of property taxes is due on December 10. Missing the deadline is a very expensive mistake, since you will incur a penalty of 10% plus a $10 fee. You can send a check, along with your payment voucher, or pay by phone. However, most people find it more convenient to pay online. The Alameda County Tax Collector’s secure URL for making payments is: https://www.acgov.org/propertytax/index.htm. If you want to use a credit card and get those frequent flyer miles, you can do so, but you pay a 2.3% processing fee (the money does NOT go to the county). A direct debit to your bank account does not incur any additional charges. You can also mail a check using the envelope provided with your bill or use your own. This year, there has been some confusion about the mailing address, since the Treasurer switched to a new payment processor in San Francisco. The Treasurer issued this clarification: 1. Use the enclosed envelopes with the current address of 1221 Oak Street, Room 131, Oakland, CA 94612. 2. Use your own envelopes with the new PO Box Address: Alameda County, Secured Property Tax Payments, PO Box 45862, San Francisco, CA 94145-0862 Finally, although there are several electronic payment services (PayPal and Venmo, to name a few) in common use these days, the Tax Collector has a specific warning about PayPal on its website: NOTICE TO TAXPAYERS USING PAYPAL At this time, we are strongly discouraging the use of PayPal for your property tax payments. Using this method of payment may result in late fees and costs. With our current technology, we can only accept full payments for property taxes; partial payments are not allowed. Wiley Hoag is the Piedmont Post Consumer Affairs reporter.

As is the case every year, Medicare Open Enrollment ends this Saturday, December 7. Medicare – which was signed into law in 1965 under President Lyndon B. Johnson – has many pieces, including Parts A, B, C (Medicare Advantage Plans), D (drug coverage), and so-called “Medigap Plans”. The details are beyond the scope of a simple newspaper article, but CMS (the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services) has a helpful fact sheet at https://www.cms.gov/files/document/2024-medicare-open-enrollment-fact-sheet.pdf If, after reading the fact sheet, your head is still spinning and you want to talk to a real human being, Medicare has a help line that is open twenty-four hours a day during open enrollment: 1-800-MEDICARE (1-800-633- 4227). It is especially important to review your Part D plan this year, as there have been many changes. Out-of-pocket cost for prescription drugs is now limited to $2,000, and the notorious “doughnut hole” has disappeared. Because of these changes, many insurance companies have raised their rates significantly. This reporter’s monthly premium for 2025 jumped by over 40%. Fortunately, using Medicare’s simple to use Part D tool, I was able to switch to another plan that was $400 a year cheaper than the renewal on my current plan. Don’t wait any longer. Go to https://www.medicare.gov/ and make sure you get the best coverage for the best price. articles.text: The City of Piedmont and Piedmont Beautification Foundation will host the annual tree-lighting celebration tonight, Wednesday, December 4, at 6:00 p.m. instead of the traditional 7 p.m. start. Lights Up Piedmont continues Piedmont’s holiday tree lighting ceremony which dates back to 1969. The event has been expanded to reflect winter light celebrations enjoyed by cultures across the globe. Piedmont Boy Scouts will be serving hot cider donated by Piedmont Grocery and hot cocoa courtesy of Heafey-Baum Group. The Recreation Department staff will also be serving hot latkes donated by Chabad Jewish Center. Parents and kids are invited to meet Santa Claus for photo opportunities inside the Community Hall following the tree being illuminated. Kids can write letters to Santa and place them in a special Santa mailbox on the plaza in front of the Community Hall. A program led by Piedmont Beautification Foundation President Patty Dunlap will begin at PBF president Patty Dunlap (left) with PBF member Julie Gardner Staff Photo A Public Works employee attaches strands of lights to the redwood tree that towers above Piedmont Community Hall. 6:00 p.m.. Music will be provided by the Troubadours, Piedmont High School’s a capella choral ensemble. A Make-A-Wish foundation recipient will flip the switch to light up the 80-foot tall redwood tree. A menorah will be installed in Piedmont Park. The Beautification Foundation dressed the park with lights bright and early on Tuesday, December 3. Piedmont Beautification Foundation and Piedmont Garden Club members smiled as they carried long strands of lights from the Community Hall to the base of the redwood tree. “We’re really excited. We expect a great crowd to kick off a very special winter season.” said Dunlap. The Piedmont Beautification Foundation maintains and keeps the lights used in the ceremony each year. Community members can support the Piedmont Beautification Foundation by donating at piedmontbeautificationfoundation.org/donate or by mailing a check to: Piedmont Beautification Foundation, City Hall, 120 Vista Avenue, Piedmont, CA 94611.

articles.text: Young Buttercream is looking for a foster or adopter. This pup is estimated to be 11 months old and is a German Shepherd mix. He is a playful dog who Oakland Animal Services staff and volunteers say likes to independently explore when outside his shelter cage. He is always happy to come to people and gently takes treats. Buttercream knows the sit command, but as a youngster is still learning his manners and would thrive with a foster or adopter willing to put in time to train him. If you are interested in fostering Buttercup, you can submit a foster application online, and/ or reach out to the fostering department at dogfostering@ oaklandsanimals.org, or drop by Oakland Animal Services on Thursday between 12-7 p.m., and Friday, Saturday, and Sunday between 12 and 3 p.m. Meet Buttercream, a year-old German Shepherd mix Potential fosters or adopters with a child younger than 12 or a dog that weighs 25 pounds, more or less than Buttercream must bring them to the shelter for the meeting. articles.text: Piedmont Makers will be hosting a jam-packed, fun-filled weekend December 7 and 8, with two Robotics events that are open to the public. Both of Piedmont’s FIRST LEGO Leagues will be gathering at Piedmont Middle School for a Festival for younger participants on Saturday and competition among. the older Makers on Sunday. Organizers expect 500-800 attendees over the course of each day. FLL Explore Festival Piedmont Makers FIRST LEGO League Explore Festival will be held Saturday, December 7. Expo #1 will be 9:30-10:30 a.m. and Expo #2 with 34 teams will be from 11:30 a.m. to 12:30 p.m. The festival will be held at Buzz Redford Gymnasium on the middle school campus. The participants will be K-3rd grade teams of six participants per team, plus coaches, parents, families, and community members. Fifty-six robotics teams will participate in two time periods. Teams will be showing their poster and project presentations, viewing the projects from other teams and giving feedback, and discussing their work with judges. The event is open to the public. FLL Challenge Community Tournament Piedmont Makers FIRST LEGO League Challenge Community Tournament is scheduled for Sunday, December 8 between 9:00 a.m. and 5:30 p.m. with competition in the John Morrison Gym on the middle school campus. Fourth through eighth graders in teams of 6-8 participants will compete, plus coaches, parents, families, and community members. A total of 36 robotics teams will participate over the course of the day. Each team will compete in four rounds of the autonomous robot game, and also present their “innovation project” to a panel of independent judges where they discuss their solution to a real world problem related to this year’s theme. articles.text: December 2, 2024 In the wake of last week’s tragedy, I have thought a lot about the remarkable strength and compassion of our community. Only in Piedmont could the annual Turkey Trot transform into a heartfelt event that provides solace and support during a time of grief. Only in Piedmont could hundreds of community members, including our students, gather for an evening vigil, united in quiet care for one another. Only in Piedmont do we come together to heal and wrap around each other in the face of sorrow. As a mother, school superintendent, and former English teacher, many of you know I regularly look to literature for wisdom and solace about how to be human. I love Naomi Shihab Nye’s poem about what it means to be a parent and what it means to care for each other in community. Parents in our community have shared insights that feel more relevant than ever at this moment: Your children are my children, and although we may not have the right words for this tragedy, our words matter. For Soren Dixon, Jack Nelson, and Krysta Tsukahara, your memories endure in our community. To grieve is to love. For Jordan Miller, we are sending good energy for a full recovery. For our families, friends, and loved ones, we share your sorrow. Grieving & Support Supporting our students and staff is front of mind for us following last week’s tragedy. Thank you to our administrators who coordinated to plan additional support for this week, along with our teachers who asked for a moment of silence this morning. And thank you to our counseling staff who have been called upon several times throughout this last month. In Community, Jennifer Hawn, Ed.D. Superintendent

articles.text: Piedmont schools reopened on Monday, December 2, and offered counseling and support for anyone with a heavy heart from the tragedy of the loss of life of three former PHS students in a car crash early Thanksgiving morning. At both the middle school and the high schools care is being offered during and after class to students. All secondary school sites have offered grief counseling during today’s December 4, mid-morning Academy period. Staff members offered to meet with students after school on Monday. “In times like these, it is natural for our children – and indeed all of us – to feel a wide range of emotions. It’s important that we come together as a community to support one another and, most importantly, our children during this difficult time,” a PUSD letter to middle school parents stated. At Piedmont High Jean Takazawa held grief circles in the lobby of Alan Harvey Theater. At the middle school an optional circle discussion was offered to help students process their emotions in a supportive setting. The offer of help was extended to staff as well. Teachers are being offered additional support to help them process this tragedy. Students are being encouraged to schedule times to talk with counselors solo or in groups at the Wellness Center. School leaders have recommended reading Miriam Warren’s article “People in Grief Need Allies” Visiblemagazine.com/ people-in-grief-need-allies/ “Grief is like being ushered behind a red velvet rope into a club no one wants membership in – but that we’ll all enter sooner or later,” Warren writes. Both schools offered the following additional resources that may help to process the tragedy that has occurred in town: Refuge in Grief Refugeingrief.com and Speaking Grief Speakinggrief. org.
articles.title: Schools offer grief counseling on Monday

articles.text: Students in the Piedmont Unified School District (PUSD) rank near the top of all school districts in California who took part in this year’s California Assessments of Student Performance and Progress (CAASPP). The CAASPP is a collection of computer-based assessments in English Language Arts/Literacy, Mathematics and now, Science. The CAASPP replaced the paper-based Standardized Testing and Reporting (STAR) program beginning in 2014. Last spring, Piedmont students in grades 3–8, and 11, participated in the 2023-24 CAASPP for English Language Arts and Math. Students in grades 5, 8, and 11 and 12, participated in the CAST Science test. “We are thrilled with the exceptional achievement of our students, and we are grateful to our teachers and staff for their outstanding work,” said Superintendent Jennifer Hawn. The California Department of Education released school, district and state aggregate results October 10. Piedmont students demonstrated remarkable achievement overall on the CAASPP, ranking third among California unified school districts in English Language Arts (ELA) and in Math, and fourth in Science. The State of California overall level of achievement in English Language Arts in 2024 was 47%. In Mathematics, the state average of meeting/exceeding was 35.5%. For Science nearly 31% of students in the state of California met or exceeded proficiency in state standards. Individual student score reports are accessed by parents electronically on the Infinite Campus Parent Portal. Directions for access are at Piedmont. k12.ca.us/default-tech/~board/ tech-support/post/infinite-campus-1676193312166 Lexile and Quantile reports are available with the student score report. A Lexile measure indicates the difficulty of materials a child can read and understand. It is based on the child’s ELA score. A Quantile measure shows what mathematical skills a student has mastered and which skills they need additional instruction in. It is based on the child’s mathematics score. The individual score reports include a link to free tools and resources in reading and mathematics. Like class assignments and report cards, the CAASPP assessments are one gauge of student progress, providing information to schools, teachers, and parents about how students perform relative to California’s goals for both learning and college and career readiness. These results will be used as one of several means to determine and meet student needs and guide discussions among parents and teachers. To see Piedmont’s full results, visit Tinyurl.com/pusdcaaspp2024 for ELA and Math, and Tinyurl. com/pusdcast2024 for Science. articles.text: To help Piedmont’s Department of Public Works keep the streets free of leaves during the fall and winter months, residents are asked to observe four rules: 1. 2. Do not put branches in the street, even small branches! They damage the street sweeping equipment. Do not sweep debris from your yard into the gutter – sweep only leaves that fall naturally into the street. 3. Sweep leaves into narrow rows outside the flow line of the gutter. Do not put them in piles. The street sweepers cannot pick up piles of leaves effectively. 4. If you want to rake your leaves, you can now add them to your weekly unlimited green waste cart. If you don’t have enough room in your cart, free compostable bags are available at City Hall to place with your green cart on garbage day. Do not bag them and then empty the bags on the street on sweeping day. Compostable bags are also available from Republic Services (1-800- 320-8077) for a fee. articles.text: Piedmont High’s cross-country team finished up its season at the CIF State Cross-Country Championship at Woodward Park in Fresno on Saturday, November 30. Sophomores Leighton Mand and Amalia Gray competed in the girls’ event, and sophomore Sebastien Swain qualified for the boys’ event for a second straight year. Piedmont competing at the State meet marked 36 consecutive years the cross country program has sent at least one athlete to the prestigious event. “Advancing to the CIF State Meet is no small feat,” explained coach Steve Zirkelbach. “Three PHS cross country athletes succeeded in qualifying to run in the Division 4 race this weekend. Seb, Leighton and Amalia capped off a great season with some good racing with the best runners in all of California.” Mand was 74th of 201 runners with a time of 19:52.7 on the 5,000-meter course. Her time was marked a personal record time by 1 minute, 18 seconds after last competing on the Woodward Park course at the 45th Annual Asics Clovis Invitational on October 12. “In her first time competing at the State Meet, Leighton came through mile one in just under six minutes, in 58th place and right in line with what she has been running in her training. About 14 runners went by her in the second mile, but she came back in 6:19 to pass two runners over the last stretch. She was the 18th fastest sophomore in her race,” Zirkelbach said. Mand emerged as the squad’s top runner this season, finishing as the girls’ team’s best runner six times in nine events this fall. Gray placed 101st with a time of 20:24.5. Her time was 46 seconds faster than her previous time at Woodward Park in October. She’s been a breakout runner as another sophomore this season. “Amalia found herself coming through the first mile in 6:05 and was in 86th place at the time. The second mile was slower due to the hills and adjusting to the quick pace of the initial mile. Only three girls were allowed to pass her in the last mile and she finished with a very good 6:36 pace to come in 101st overall. She was the 23rd fastest sophomore in the Div. 4 race,” Zirkelbach said. Leighton Mand (1362) finished the D4 CIF State Cross Country Championship in 74th of 201 runners with a time of 19:52.7. Amalia Gray (1361) placed 101st with a time of 20:24.5 on the State Championship as a sophomore. Sebastien Swain, a sophomore, ran in his second State Cross Country Championship and finished 96th.

articles.text: Piedmont High played its first official game at Binks Rawlings Gym on Saturday, November 30, bashing the visiting Gateway Gators 81-54. It was a productive game for PHS’ offense with eight different scorers. “It was a good start; we had balanced scoring all the way through. We shot 56 percent from the field,” coach Ben Spencer said. Dillon Casey led the way with 26 points, while senior guard Ravi Silverberg put up 19. “Dillon and Ravi both had a big game. Akash Bornstein also got us going with his energy off of the bench. P.J. Brayer was strong on the glass and Lucian Fang Ring made a big 3-pointer at the end of the first half to give us momentum,” Spencer said. The Highlanders now look ahead to the start of its Winter Classic at home from Thursday, December 5 through Saturday, December 7. Piedmont gets things started against Envision Academy. “We have Hayward, Head Royce, AIMS from Oakland, Envision, Acalanes, Westmoore and Northgate. It’s a pretty good lineup. The semifinals and finals will be very good games and we’ll have another really competitive tournament,” Spencer said. Game Recap PHS held a narrow 20-14 lead through the first quarter and extended to a 12-point gap in the second to 37-25 by halftime. The Highlanders then scored 24 points in the third quarter and allowed 15 to go up 61-40, adding 20 more points in the final going toward the 81-54 victory. In the first quarter, Casey put up eight of his team’s 20 points while Silverberg scored four. Emmett Asulin, Beach Lorin, Brayer, and Fang Ring added individual baskets. Fang Ring led the way in the second quarter by knocking down a pair of 3-pointers, including one to end the first half. articles.text: This year’s Piedmont High football team finished its season 10-2 overall with a Division 7 Semifinal berth in the North Coast Section playoffs after winning the Western Alameda County Conference Mission Division title by going 5-0. A question recently was asked: Was this year’s football team better than the 2021 undefeated squad, which played only five games in the Covid-shortened season. The Highlanders’ football team played its season in the spring after California brought back sports in March of 2021. The football was one of the most successful programs at the school, finishing its season at 5-0 in the WACC’s newly formed Mission Division under head coach Jerome Johnson. Had there been an NCS Playoffs, Piedmont would have been the No. 1 seed in Division 4, NCS added opened divisions 6 and 7 in 2019 for small school enrollment. Piedmont competed in Div. 7 and this year was promoted to Div. 6. The Highlanders’ wins included a 20-14 in double overtime over Castro Valley, 42-7 against Mt. Eden, a 33-0 shutout of Berkeley, another shutout 21-0 over Washington, and a 14-12 win over Kennedy. 2021 was a big season for senior running back Brian Cain, who was named Honorable Mention for Athlete of the Year by the Post after recording 721 rushing yards on 122 attempts to average 5.91 yards per carry with 15 total touchdowns. He averaged an astonishing 144.2 yards per game and would’ve been on-pace for 1,442 yards on a full 10-game regular season—not counting NCS games. Photo by Ken DeCrosta Running back Brian Cain was the Post’s 2021 Honorable Mention for Athlete of the Year after averaging an eye-popping 144.2 yards per game and three touchdowns per game. Cain was a factor in each game as the bell cow of Piedmont’s offense. He had 229 yards and four touchdowns against Mt. Eden, 180 yards and three touchdowns on Washington, 102 yards and three touchdowns on Berkeley, 119 yards and two touchdowns on Kennedy, and 91 yards, two touchdowns, and an interception return for a touchdown on Castro Valley, With Cain on offense, the Highlanders found they could lean on its defense to capitalize in key situations. Similar to Jordan Alemania’s support on Piedmont’s defensive line this year, 2021’s Highlanders had Andy Melian as an edge and interior rusher. He finished the 2021 shortened season with seven sacks and 16 tackles for loss. Melian wreaked havoc over Castro Valley with 11 total tackles, two sacks, seven tackles for loss, and a block extra point. He also put up two sacks on Kennedy and another two sacks and four tackles for loss on Washington. Melian went on to play football at Kenyon College in Ohio. In the season-finale against Kennedy, the defense had 10 tackles for loss and two stops in the redzone. The football program returned for the fall 2021 semester with a depleted roster, appearing with just 16-20 student-athletes each game. They finished 2-7 overall in Johnson’s last season in the fall of 2021, which led to former athletic director Bradley Smet abruptly canceling the football season going into 2022 and PHS losing its position within the WACC league. After parents rallied to revive the program, PHS returned for 2022 under Jordan Seiden as an independent team and started 0-4 against stout competition before canceling the varsity program due to low roster availability. Piedmont returned to the WACC’s Shoreline Division, its lowest level, in 2023 and captured the title by going 5-1 in league and 7-4 overall—falling to Alhambra in the first round of the D5 postseason. After securing the Mission Division title in 2024, it’s still unclear if PHS will be promoted, once again. The Highlanders played in the WACC’s top echelon, the Foothill, from 2016-2019. Photo by Todd Marshburn Piedmont’s defense was led by Andy Melian (58), who played as a defensive and offensive lineman.

articles.text: Opera composer Gioachino Rossini The great opera composer Gioachino Rossini set the world on fire. We all know him as a delightful composer of such operas as The Barber of Seville. He was also a noted humorist. As such, he was a diplomat of the highest order. He retired at an early age and dabbled as a host for famous musical parties. But did you know that this great composer was also a famous gourmand? The most famous dish which bears his name is tornadoes of beef a la Rossini. Prepare yourselves for a post-Thanksgiving treat. Exactly one week after attending a disappointing concert in Indianapolis played by one of the current “superstars” of the music world, I attended a concert by four local musicians. Let me be completely honest with you, Many of these superstars are technically adapt, but musically lacking. Perfection, as such doesn’t do very much for me. Somehow they have forgotten the human aspect in their quest for perfection. A concert Saturday in our Piedmont Center for the Arts filled all of the requirements. The program featuring Trio Solano with pianist Miles Graber was just that. It was curated by local violinist and art collector Dan Flanagan, who is a true renaissance man. Musically, he is an outstanding violinist and a composer to boot. To this impressive dossier, he is also an art connoisseur of the highest order. In the concert he was joined by the outstanding violist, Paul Ehrlich, and his equally outstanding wife Vicky Erlich on the cello. They were featured in Flanagan’s original composition entitled Tamayo and Beethoven’s superb String Trio No. 1 during the first half of the concert. What is unique about Flanagan’s programs is that he combines excellent music with carefully selected art projections. The second half of the concert featured the world premiere of a composition by Cindy Cox, and a superlative rendition of Dvořák’s Piano Quartet in E flat major, which is about as close to a concerto grosso as this great Bohemian composer had ever written. The reason I prefer “aspiring artists” is that they have a human element. The Musical Gourmet The Musical Gourmet He writes that he has completed one of the most monumental works for the guitar. He was inspired by the 24 preludes and fugues by Johann Sebastian Bach. Torrent has written 24 Preludes and fugues in every key imaginable. Guitarists generally play in two keys, E and A. When they play in another key, they often re-tune the guitar or use artificial means. They rarely venture into other keys. They would be well advised to open their horizons. Perhaps Torrent will play a concert in our PCA and demonstrate his newest compositions. Returning to Rossini for a moment, I remember something that he wrote. He observed that he cried only three times in his life. The first time was when his first opera failed. The second time was when he heard the great violinist Niccolo Paganini play. And the third time was when he was on a boarding party and a truffled turkey fell into the water. When I was very young. I didn’t know what a truffled turkey was. My thinking was, didn’t the turkey know how to swim or fly. Many years later I learned what truffles were, and that a turkey in the early 1800s was extremely expensive in Europe. Well… Thanksgiving is over and the mad rush to the end of the year has just begun. Rossini’s truffled turkey inspires me to give you an idea. I hope you have some turkey leftovers. What follows is a unique Turkey recipe that is completely original. RECIPE Prepare a sauce made with a little bit of olive oil, a tablespoon of capers with some juice, a tablespoon of Mediterranean olives with some juice and a little bit of sour cream. Season to taste with some salt and pepper, and perhaps some poultry seasoning. And now the unusual ingredient. Add a tablespoon of Dijon mustard to each portion. Mix thoroughly and warm the turkey in this delectable sauce. Bon appétit. How about this recipe maestro Rossini? Sean Connery and Rob Brown in Finding Forrester Finding Forrester is simply a wonderful film which not only explores an unexpected friendship between a reclusive novelist William Forrester, portrayed by Sean Connery, and a local high school student Jamal Wallace, so well acted by Rob Brown. In the opening scenes we see Jamal and his Bronx friends playing basketball, almost daily, on a neighborhood court. Forrester, from his third floor corner apartment window, often watches, binoculars in hand. His presence doesn’t go unnoticed by Jamal and friends as they banter and shoot hoops below. We soon learn that Jamal is not only a talented player, but a gifted writer and voracious reader and fills notebooks and journals with stories which he carries in his backpack while cradling his ever present basketball. It is when Jamal accepts a dare from his cohort that Forrester and Jamal have an unexpected encounter. Late one night, his backpack on his shoulder, Jamal climbs the exterior fire escape and opens a window and crawls into the dark apartment, much of it obscured. He slowly walks from room to room, taking a letter opener, proving he was there. Forrester leaps out of the darkness, scaring Jamal, causing him to drop his backpack and bolt for the apartment’s front door. It’s at this point in the narrative that the relationship between Jamal and Forrester truly takes hold and becomes the essence of the film. First things first: his backpack containing the journals. Finding Forrester is so good and softly engaging; it is one of the best films about writing that I have ever encountered. It also features a tour de force performance by F. Murray Abraham as a self-important English professor who is intent on diminishing Jamal’s love of language while ridiculing/stereotyping his talent on the court. Finding Forrester. articles.text: The term B movie was long used to refer to those second tier films that ran after the main attraction during the 40s and 50s. In fact, to make sure audiences felt like they received sufficient bang for their buck, going to the movies meant watching a newsreel a cartoon and two feature The Bs were hurry-up movies with less well-known stars, small budgets, and were the equivalent of those dime magazines widely popular during the same time period known as pulp fiction. The paper between the covers was rough and cheap (pulpy), the subjects running to gritty detective mysteries, wildly imagined tales of science fiction and melodramatic westerns. This is all to say that instead of calling a film such as Edge of Darkness a B movie (and all the films of that ilk), it might be more accurate to simply call it pulp cinema. That’s not to imply that such films are not entertaining. Indeed, lacking all pretense, with stripped down plots and dialogue, pulpy movies can entertain and then some. pages.text: Wednesday, December 4, 2024 19 MOVIES FOR ADULTS Finding Forrester a gem with Sean Connery Edge of Darkness – excellent pulp film By Chris Honoré The term B movie was long used to refer to those second tier films that ran after the main attraction during the 40s and 50s. In fact, to make sure audiences felt like they received sufficient bang for their buck, going to the movies meant watching a newsreel a cartoon and two feature films. The Bs were hurry-up movies with less well-known stars, small budgets, and were the equivalent of those dime magazines widely popular during the same time period known as pulp fiction. The paper between the covers was rough and cheap (pulpy), the subjects running to gritty detective mysteries, wildly imagined tales of science fiction and melodramatic westerns. This is all to say that instead of calling a film such as Edge of Darkness a B movie (and all the films of that ilk), it might be more accurate to simply call it pulp cinema. In the opening scenes we see Jamal and his Bronx friends playing basketball, almost daily, on a neighborhood court. Forrester, from his third floor corner apartment window, often watches, binoculars in hand. His presence doesn’t go unnoticed by Jamal and friends as they banter and shoot hoops below. We soon learn that Jamal is not only a talented player, but a gifted writer and voracious reader and fills notebooks and journals with stories which he carries in his backpack while cradling his ever present basketball. It is when Jamal accepts a dare from his cohort that Forrester and Jamal have an unexpected encounter. Late one night, his backpack on his shoulder, Jamal climbs the exterior fire escape and opens a window and crawls into the dark apartment, much of it obscured. He slowly walks from room to room, taking a letter opener, proving he was there. Forrester leaps out of the darkness, scaring Jamal, causing him to drop his backpack and bolt for the apartment’s front door. It’s at this point in the narrative that the relationship between Jamal and Forrester truly takes hold and becomes the essence of the film. First things first: his backpack containing the journals. Finding Forrester is so good and softly engaging; it is one of the best films about writing that I have ever encountered. It also features a tour de force performance by F. Murray Abraham as a self-important English professor who is intent on diminishing Jamal’s love of language while ridiculing/stereotyping his talent on the court. Finding Forrester. articles.text: A scene from Disney Pixar’s Cars What Disney discovered a century ago is that kids are not only a large and loyal audience, but they are a forgiving one, meaning they willingly and enthusiastically suspend their disbelief. What this means is that the groundbreaking studio Disney, founded in the early 20th century, could, as part of their rich, animated storytelling, give animals and inanimate objects human characteristics, often described as anthropomorphism. Disney released its first animated short, Steamboat Willie, in 1928, starring a now iconic, big-eared mouse named Mickey, and the company, to include a deep bench of producers, animators, and storytellers have never looked back. Today, Disney Animation Studios includes Pixar, Marvel Studios, Lucasfilms, 20th Century Animation, and Searchlight. It is the much acclaimed and award-winning Pixar, now a subsidiary of Disney, which produced the computer-animated series Cars (1-3), introducing Lighting McQueen (Owen Wilson), a rookie, cocky racecar on his way to a tie-breaking Piston Cup race in California. Unexpectedly, he ends up stuck in a sleepy retro-town (1950s) called Radiator Springs, a forgotten burg just off of Route 66. Due to his reckless, hurry-up attitude, he is informed that he can’t leave town until he helps repair Main Street. During his reluctant layover, McQ. meets the local characters such as tow truck Mater (Larry the Cable Guy), not the sharpest nail around; the owner of the Corvette Motel, Sally (Bonnie Hunt); and the much esteemed retired champion racer, Doc Hudson (Paul Newman). At first McQ. is eager to get out of Radiator Springs; however, forced to slow his racecar pace, meaning his life in the fast lane, he gradually realizes that slowing down is appealing, as are the friendships he develops with the town’s denizens. He enjoys hanging out with the likes of Doc Hudson and Mater…and, of course, there’s Sally. And so McQ. learns a nice life lesson. And there is the extraordinary signature emotive animation for which Pixar is well known. Kids will love Cars, and they’ll be happy to know that there are two more waiting in the wings. Vroom vroom. Cars. Directed by John Lasseter, Joe Ronft. Voiced by Owen Wilson, Paul Newman, Bonnie Hunt. Walt Disney/Pixar animation. 1 hr., 57 min. Rated G. Streaming on Fandango/prime/ Disney+/apple tv. Released in 2006.

articles.text: Every winter I cozy up on the couch and gaze out the window onto my leaf scattered backyard dreaming of what I’ll plant next year. It’s the perfect time to let your soil rest and for gardeners to choose next year’s seeds. Here are a few tips for selecting the best varieties so your seed library is fully stocked and ready for spring. The right crops for your garden are always the ones you want Michelle Docter chooses seeds for next year’s spring garden. to grow. Yet, maybe you’re not picking the right variety for your space. Take note of plants that gave you abundant, delicious harvests as well as crops that were stunted, succumbed to pests, or just weren’t that flavorful. Taking notes in a garden notebook each season can help you understand how crops grow in your garden over time. This can help you choose varieties that may suit your space better in consideration of heat and disease resistant varieties or crops with a different flavor profile. During this off-season think about how you’ll plant out next year’s garden beds. Consider rotating crop families in different locations to help rebuild your soil. Try companion planting by sowing crops together that benefit from one another, such as basil and tomatoes. This pre-planning will give you a better idea of what you may want to grow even before you make your first purchase of seeds. Starting plants from seed is a labor of love, so you want seeds that will germinate well. Here are a few trustworthy seed companies I purchase from that offer a wide selection of successful seeds: • Renee’s Garden Seed Company • Botanical Interests • High Mowing Organic Seeds • Johnny’s Selected Seeds • Plant Good Seed Company If you’d rather buy plant starts, opt for your local nursery over big box stores. They’ll likely have more options with better cared for plants. If you’re anything like me, I can get carried away with dreaming up so many crop varieties. My advice is to think about your garden space and what will actually fit. Just keep in mind you can try one variety this year and switch it up next year. That’s the joy of gardening – there’s always room for experimentation to see what amazing things might grow. Girl And Her Dog Farm is run by backyard farmer, Michelle Docter in Albany, CA. articles.text: One of the happiest pleasures of movies is seeing one with friends and then chatting about it when the lights come up. That’s just what Piedmont’s Flix Fest offers: a great movie in a comfortable setting on the second Thursday of each month and then a lively discussion afterward. December’s offering is one of the most beloved of American romantic comedy classics: 1953’s Roman Holiday. Directed by William Wyler, it earned its female lead a Best Actress Academy Award. We all know her name: Audrey Hepburn. It’s hard to believe that, before she starred in Roman Holiday, Audrey Hepburn was not well known. She had appeared for about one minute as Alec Guiness’s daughter, Chiquita (!), in The Lavender Hill Mob, and in a few other films. She was a dancer, as well. Most people forget that in 1953 she won another important award, a Tony for Ondine. And then came Roman Holiday, earning her instant worldwide stardom. Who can resist her delicate charm? Of course her co-star, Gregory Peck, had already risen to entertainment heights. Together they make irresistible the story of a princess who, itching to escape her restricted life, decides to take a holiday from it by sneaking out into the bustle of modern Rome. Peck plays the American newspaper guy who discovers who she is and, pretending ignorance in order to get a scoop, takes her on a breezy tour of the Eternal City. (Watch for the scene in which a giant stone head bites off Peck’s hand—it’s classic.) Of course their time together turns into a love story, but can an ordinary guy possibly get a girl who’s a princess? A factoid: Hepburn may have had a leg up in playing a princess: her mother was a baroness. Roman Holiday will be screened on December 12th at 1:00 p.m. The event takes place in the Center for the Arts at 801 Magnolia Avenue on the second Thursday of each month. Doors will open at 12:45. The event is free and open to anyone over 18 years of age. Participants are invited on a drop-in basis, though registration can be done at https:// bit.ly/3PJyxkP. Everyone is welcome to bring snacks or lunch. The next movie in the Piedmont series is the far-out Mel Brooks comedy/western, Blazing Saddles. It will be shown on January 9th.

articles.text: On Thanksgiving Eve and members of the Walking on Wednesdays group showed up 27 strong to enjoy the weather, being together, and work on their Thanksgiving dinner appetites, with Jim Kellogg leading the way. They knew about 2,400 runners and walkers were going to be on the same streets the next morning for the annual Piedmont Turkey Trot. The group would walk the Turkey Trot route one day before Thanksgiving and be the first across the race finish line. Thanksgiving is the biggest U.S. running day of the year. Last year an estimated 920,761 people participated in 833 races across the country. The Piedmont Turkey Trot is conducted by a non-profit that supports organizations promoting school cross-country and track for both high school and middle school. It would be the 23rd year for the Piedmont Turkey Trot which started in 2001 with 300 runners. Participation was as high as 3,100 one year, and since then has been capped at 2400 entries. Awards are given for the top three male and female finishers in nine age divisions from youth to over-80. Last year’s Piedmont Turkey Trot was won by Piedmont High grad Jack Stein in 15-minutes, 30-seconds on the 3-mile course on city streets. The walkers did not think they would challenge Jack’s time, but they would do the entire Turkey Trot route of 5 kilometers. Before the group started their walk, Jim Kellogg shared a sad announcement that Will Adams, one of their well-respected Wednesday Walkers, unexpectedly passed away the prior week. The group all remembers Will for his smile and his friendly and positive personality, as well as being a very talented architect, urban planners and architectural historian who several times guided the walkers on tours of notable Piedmont buildings. Will is also remembered for authoring the Walking Piedmont, Observations of the Built Environment of a Beautiful City columns in the Piedmont Post. He will be greatly missed by all. The walkers experienced the entire route of the Trot They continued up the long “Heartbreak Hill” climb on Sea View Avenue, then floated down Mountain Avenue to the finish line at the Exedra. In a contested finish, Jim Kellogg and Bob Wong pulled away in the home stretch to be the first Wednesday Walkers to cross the imagined finish line. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 a.m. Everyone is invited to join the group and there is no charge. New walkers and their friendly K-9 best friends are especially welcome. Register at https://tinyurl. com/3ethkehu. Among those on hand for a walk last Wednesday were Denny McGee, Marion Lim Yankowitz, Mark Davis and Noemi Alvarado, Jack and Sharona Fischrup, Tom Lehrkind, Alan Goldhammer, Elizabeth Richter, Edith Lee, Bill Ahern, June Yee, Karin Fetherston, Jim Kuo, Karen Palmer, Judy Love, Kat Lang, Sherry Jacobs, Bob Wong, Mary Henderson, Jim Kellogg, Brian Henderson, Tina Shum, Claudine Bach, Stella Houston, and Priscilla Wanerus.

articles.text: William P. Adams Jr., 77, died peacefully surrounded by family Wednesday, November 20, 2024, in Piedmont, California. Will was born June 1, 1947 in Oakland, California to William and Rose Mary Adams, the second born of 6 children. His beloved brother Stephan Adamczyk and sister-In-Law Patricia preceded him in death. Will was raised in Richmond, CA. He enjoyed a 45-year career as an Architect and Planner in the San Francisco Bay Area. His work took him to projects all over the US, including Hawaii and Alaska, and internationally in Canada, Mexico, Costa Rica, the Virgin Islands, Cayman Islands, Korea, China, Dubai, and Morocco. He enjoyed making presentations to diverse groups, (including elementary and high school classes) serving on several design review boards in both Colorado and California, and taking time to raise public awareness about the built environment. He was passionate about teaching others the importance of designing places that facilitate and encourage community. Will authored “The Alphabet of Architecture - a primer on the built environment” (2010), a cherished book filled with his drawings and immense knowledge. He had a love of hand drawings which had been a tool to design projects of many different types and sizes over his career. A former colleague writes, “We all benefited from his immense talent, his compassion and empathy, his unwavering integrity…He had a profound influence producing innovative design solutions to complex problems that were illustrated with clarity and beauty. Much of his design philosophy and approach lives on today. I’m a better professional from knowing and working with him, and I know I’ve been enriched by his admirable qualities as a person…” Will had a memorable, special way he connected with people. His deep listening skills promoted wise questions that would guide someone to their own conclusions. He never criticized, always encouraged, respecting others thoughts without judgement. He had a talent of recognizing the different abilities within She said, “I’ve learned that whenever I decide something with an open heart, I usually make the right decision. I’ve learned that even when I have pains, I don’t have to be one. I’ve learned that every day you should reach out and touch someone. People love a warm hug, or just a friendly pat on the back. I’ve learned that I still have a lot to learn. I’ve learned that people will forget what you did, but people will never forget how you made them feel. – Maya Angelou Will Adams lived a life filled with the meaning of love. Our beloved Will, you are cherished and will be profoundly missed. Will is survived by his wife Linda Adams, daughter Alissa, granddaughter Chelsea Rose and son-in-law Christopher (“Chris”) Richardson. He is also survived by his sister Catherine Adams Koster (Steve) and brothers Michael (“Mike”) Adams, Mark Adams (Vanessa), and Tony Adams (Virginia). Will was a cherished uncle to his nieces and nephews Andrea, Amanda, Carly, Corby, Tom, Jesse, Kailey, Fae, Theo, Geordie, Ronan, and Rory. On learning of his passing one niece wrote “Losing someone so pivotal to our family has been truly difficult. Uncle Will had a quiet and steady manner. He was insightful, expressive and truly curious about us as individuals…” A special thank-you to dear friends Elizabeth Brady and Inna Rand for their kind assistance with these memories. A Memorial Service will be held on Saturday, March 8th (time to be determined) at Piedmont Community Church. In lieu of flowers, donations can be made to the Piedmont Community Church in Will’s name.

Ultimately, he had a way of making a person feel seen. He was a true friend and touched every moment with kindness. He even had a special touch with animals, his family cats giving him kisses and the birds finding sanctuary in the garden. Will was an incredibly humorous man who filled every gathering with laughter. As a child he would love to play pranks on his brothers, leaving them hanging for awhile, finally all would join in with a laugh. Sometimes Will’s infectious humor was fabulously dry, other times highlighting the absurdity of things. He was a closet Three Stooges fan but hid it for career reasons! Excelling in high school, Will lettered in baseball, tennis, and basketball, and was voted Class President. He studied Latin, which assisted his later mastering of the German and Spanish languages. He attended USC on full academic and athletic scholarship (tennis), transferring to UC Berkeley to complete his Bachelor of Architecture. Will and Linda enjoyed skiing, sailing, traveling, snorkeling, crossword puzzles and ballroom and folk dancing together. Will also enjoyed scuba diving (certified), soccer coaching and refereeing for Piedmont teams, starting with his daughter’s team. In October 2019, he walked 165 miles of the famous pilgrimage trail, El Camino de Santiago, Spain, from Astorga (circa de León) to Santiago de Compostela. He carried only a few carefully selected Prisma pencils, yet still filled an entire sketchbook. At one point on the trail, Will could not stop thinking about a special moment he saw. He backtracked two miles to revisit that perfect spot and sketched a magical moment which was beautiful in its simplicity. Will was active in the Piedmont Community Church, serving as President, Chairman of Deacons, and Team Leader for Youth Trips to Mexico, where he resourcefully procured non-electric tools for the group’s rural home construction projects. He also contributed artwork for various Church projects, and taught Sunday School for many years. Piedmont held a special place in Will’s heart. He was an avid neighborhood walker, and authored 76 bi-monthly “Walking Piedmont” columns in the local newspaper that discussed and promoted walkability and aesthetic sensibilities and encouraged a sense of community among his neighbors. In 2018, Will shared a favorite poem. No doubt, he lived a life true to every word.

Will was an incredibly humorous man who filled every gathering with laughter. Excelling in high school, Will lettered in baseball, tennis, and basketball, and was voted Class President. He studied Latin, which assisted his later mastering of the German and Spanish languages. He attended USC on full academic and athletic scholarship (tennis), transferring to UC Berkeley to complete his Bachelor of Architecture. Will and Linda enjoyed skiing, sailing, traveling, snorkeling, crossword puzzles and ballroom and folk dancing together. Will also enjoyed scuba diving (certified), soccer coaching and refereeing for Piedmont teams, starting with his daughter’s team. In October 2019, he walked 165 miles of the famous pilgrimage trail, El Camino de Santiago, Spain, from Astorga (circa de León) to Santiago de Compostela. He carried only a few carefully selected Prisma pencils, yet still filled an entire sketchbook. At one point on the trail, Will could not stop thinking about a special moment he saw. He backtracked two miles to revisit that perfect spot and sketched a magical moment which was beautiful in its simplicity. Will was active in the Piedmont Community Church, serving as President, Chairman of Deacons, and Team Leader for Youth Trips to Mexico, where he resourcefully procured non-electric tools for the group’s rural home construction projects. He also contributed artwork for various Church projects, and taught Sunday School for many years. Piedmont held a special place in Will’s heart. He was an avid neighborhood walker, and authored 76 bi-monthly “Walking Piedmont” columns in the local newspaper that discussed and promoted walkability and aesthetic sensibilities and encouraged a sense of community among his neighbors. In 2018, Will shared a favorite poem. No doubt, he lived a life true to every word. She said, “I’ve learned that whenever I decide something with an open heart, I usually make the right decision. I’ve learned that I still have a lot to learn. I’ve learned that people will forget what you did, but people will never forget how you made them feel. – Maya Angelou Will Adams lived a life filled with the meaning of love. Our beloved Will, you are cherished and will be profoundly missed. Will was a cherished uncle to his nieces and nephews Andrea, Amanda, Carly, Corby, Tom, Jesse, Kailey, Fae, Theo, Geordie, Ronan, and Rory. She was born in Honolulu, Hawaii, on May 9th, 1937 and. throughout her life she exemplified the true Aloha spirit, radiating warmth, generosity and an unforgettable laugh. Eddy was a bright student and a natural athlete who thrived in swimming and tennis programs offered by the local parks. Her mother, Kalani, was a nurse and early on worked at the Kalaupapa settlement on Molokai established by Father Damien to treat Hansen’s disease patients. After elementary school, Eddy enrolled in the Kamehameha Schools, which were established for children of Hawaiian descent. At Kamehameha, she developed her writing skills in the school newspaper and the school annual and her athletic skills primarily on the tennis team. In her senior year of high school she was selected as a member of the National Honor Society and the Quill and Scroll Society. In retirement, she would honor her school by co-authoring a book highlighting the achievements of prominent graduates of Kamehameha Schools. Upon graduation, Eddy enrolled in the University of Hawaii and graduated with a degree in Sociology. She then pursued a master’s degree in social work at the University of passion for education and her students were a hallmark of her life. Her colleagues and students admired her dedication, patience and leadership. In addition to her career, Eddy’s contributions to the East Bay Children’s Theater were a source of great satisfaction and pride. She was twice president of the organization, and was fully committed to the 90-year tradition of EBCT – to bring the joy of live musical theater to the underserved schools of the East Bay. After moving to Piedmont in1978, Eddy was soon involved in the neighborhood organization which had developed around the triangle block of Bonita, Ramona and Estrella and was instrumental in organizing a directory, coordinating the yearly block parties on the 4th of July and around Christmas time and meetings related to emergency preparedness. A true soprano, singing was a true passion of hers and she was a loyal member of the St. Theresa Choir until her health declined. Eddy and Don were lifelong tennis partners and members of the Berkeley Tennis Club for over 40 years. News of the fatal event quickly spread. At 9:30 a.m. on Wednesday, November 27, Police Chief Jeremy Bowers and Fire Chief Dave Brannigan held a press conference for media outlets. “I really want to keep the focus on the victims and the families that have lost their loved ones,” Bowers said. “I will tell you that our women and men who responded to this call did everything they could.” Speed is believed to have resulted in the crash. Investigations are being conducted by the California Highway Patrol and National Highway Traffic Safety Administration. 1 classmate survives A fourth classmate, Jordan Miller, was removed from the wreck by a motorist that was following behind the Cybertruck. “There was a motorist that was traveling behind the vehicle that was involved in the collision, a significant distance behind that vehicle. And when they turned the corner they saw the vehicle in flames, [then] a person exited that vehicle and helped extract one of the involved parties out of the vehicle [on fire],” explained Bowers. “It’s good to know that somebody was willing to help. They probably saved a life,” said Brannigan. A City in mourning The following day, a moment of silence was conducted before the start of the annual five kilometer Turkey Trot run on Piedmont streets, and a memorial was made at the site of the crash. The course of the Turkey Trot run was altered to allow runners to pay their respects. More than 1500 flowers were placed at the crash site as a memorial. The Turkey Trot served in many ways as a walking procession, and communal expression of grief. Sandy Martin, a 6th grade teacher, and Piedmonter Aileen Desoto appeared on KGO Channel 7 news.
